body: ## Motivation ZTF DR2 analysis finds evidence for a broken stretch-luminosity relation. BBC assumed one global alpha and a single-alpha bias correction, so it could not separate a genuine broken standardization from a wrong-model biasCor artifact. This issue tracked adding two-slope alpha support to SALT2mu/BBC and validating it on sims; ## Implemented (merged: PRs #1753, #1754, #1757) alpha(x1) = alpha1 + (alpha0 - alpha1) * S((x1 - x1_cen)/x1_tau), with S the sigmoid: alpha1 applies below the pivot, alpha0 above, and x1_tau = 0 is a hard step. - `u24=1` activates the second slope; p24 to p27 = alpha1, dalpha1/dz, x1_cen, x1_tau (aliases `alpha1=`, `dalpha_dz=`, `x1_cen=`, `x1_tau=`). p24 needs an explicit init value. - BiasCor uses each event's own alpha,beta in the mu-residual path when the second slope is active; single-alpha fits keep the legacy common alpha,beta (a later update may retire the legacy path). - New YAML keys `COV_alpha0_alpha1`, `RHO_alpha0_alpha1`, and a warning when a fitted parameter sits at or near a MINUIT bound. - Regression task `SALT2mu_ZTFSIM_BROKEN_ALPHA` added to SNANA_TESTS. ## Validation sims All sims use the GENPDF SNVAR-conditioning of PR #1749: SALT2ALPHA drawn per event from P(alpha | x1), with the break and a small scatter (0.0032) encoded in the map, and SIM_alpha recording the truth. - Data sims (SALT3.K21-Frag, G10, ~20k generated, 1800 to 2000 after cuts): single-alpha control at 0.15; published-amplitude break, alpha 0.215/0.085 at x1 = -0.25; doubled break, 0.280/0.020. - BiasCor maps: fixed alpha = 0.15 (500k); alpha-beta grid, nodes 0.1/0.2 x 2.6/3.6 (2M); widened 0.02/0.28 grid (2M), since the branch alphas fall outside 0.1 to 0.2 and would clamp at the edge nodes. - Nine baseline single-alpha BBC fits (every data sim x every map) as reference FITRES/M0DIF. ## Results (sim only) All fits: master `v12_02-143-g52f6382`, widened 2x2 grid, `opt_biascor=4336`, `fitflag_sigmb=2`, pivot and width floated unless noted. Full outputs with one `CMD.txt` per fit are group readable on Midway at `/scratch/midway2/tztang/ISSUE1751_RESULTS_20260811`. | data sim | injected alpha1 / alpha0 | fitted alpha1 | fitted alpha0 | alpha1 - alpha0 | CHI2RED_IA | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | no break | 0.150 / 0.150 | 0.1450 +/- 0.0050 | 0.1486 +/- 0.0055 | -0.0036 +/- 0.0088 (0.4 sigma) | 0.995 | | published break | 0.215 / 0.085 | 0.2080 +/- 0.0053 | 0.0837 +/- 0.0063 | +0.1243 +/- 0.0092 (13.5 sigma) | 0.984 | | doubled break | 0.280 / 0.020 | 0.2815 +/- 0.0053 | 0.0154 +/- 0.0056 | +0.2661 +/- 0.0091 (29.3 sigma) | 0.954 | Difference errors use the fitted covariance (rho is -0.2 to -0.4 here, so plain quadrature would overstate the significance). The no-break row is the null test: the second slope does not fabricate a break. For contrast, the single-alpha fits on the same broken sims return one averaged slope, 0.1482 +/- 0.0042 (published) and 0.1556 +/- 0.0045 (doubled), and leave the break-scaled V in the Hubble residuals shown in the first plot; the two-slope fit removes it (binned-mean RMS 0.131 to 0.028). Sigmoid pivot and width, doubled-break sim (the published amplitude at 2000 events does not constrain the pivot, x1_cen = +0.15 +/- 0.17, expected since the pivot lever scales with N * Delta_alpha^2): | fit | x1_cen | x1_tau | |---|---|---| | width floated | -0.2312 +/- 0.0286 | rails at the 0.05 minimum | | width fixed at 0.15 | -0.2180 +/- 0.0562 | fixed | | width fixed at 0.30 | -0.1811 +/- 0.0735 | fixed | | width fixed at 0.50 | -0.1107 +/- 0.0867 | fixed | - The floated-width fit lands 0.7 sigma from the injected pivot -0.25, inside the transition band the sim actually realizes (-0.242 to -0.206 from finite x1 sampling). The width correctly runs to its lower bound, since the injected truth is a hard step, and the new guard reports it: `WARNING(exec_mnpout_mnerrs): x1_tau = 0.050000 is railed at MINUIT bound [0.050,9.000]`. - Restarting the pivot from +0.25 instead of -0.75 reproduces the result to every printed digit. With a hard step the pivot chi2 was piecewise constant and the fitted pivot depended on its start; the sigmoid is what makes it fittable. - Fixed-width fits drift by about +0.3 * x1_tau, the expected offset when a sigmoid is fitted to a hard-step truth; extrapolating to zero width points back at the injected pivot. - On the no-break sim a floated pivot is correctly unconstrained (x1_cen = +1.7 +/- 1.0) and the same near-bound warning fires.

comments.body:
Back in April 2026, issue https://github.com/RickKessler/SNANA/issues/1649 
changed the number of stored hosts from MXHOSTGAL = 2 -> 3. While the number of written hosts is truncated, NMATCH and NMATCH2 record total number of matches. In the DES-SN5YR DR, only 2 hosts were recorded, but SNID=1432026 has NMATCH=3. WIth current MXHOSTGAL=3, the 3rd host has all zeros, leading to log(0) somewhere in the HOST_CONFUSION (HC) computation. The fix for defining HC arguments is to define a local NMATCH2_DEFINED counter (snana.F90) that increments only if SNHOST_OBJID(igal) != 0, so that suppressed hosts are excluded from the HC calculation. This logic should be robust if MXHOSTGAL is increased in the future.

Added stdout warning:
HOST_CONFUSION WARNING: NMATCH2= 3 but only 2 HOSTS recorded for CID=1432026
but there is nothing in the output SNANA or FITRES table to indicate loss of information for HC.

New DES-SN5YR sims will record all three hosts and thus provide a more correct HC calculation compared to the real-data DR in which only 2 of the 3 hosts go into the HC calculation. To enable a more accurate sim for NMATCH=3 events, I may add a new sim-input key
MXHOSTGAL_FORCE: 2
Unfortunately there is no clear way to automate this feature, and thus users would have to remember adding this key if the HC calculation is important.

body: There are nearly 200k LSST objects in FASTDB, and searching for spec-confirmed 2006ctw in the extracted data files seemed to be taking a bit long, reading about about 800 events/sec on RCC/Midway. Anticipating much bigger data sets, reading thru 1 million events to find your favorite event (e.g. using SNCCID_LIST) would take about 20 minutes, and any kind of debugging on such an event would be almost impossible.

comments.body: To see what was taking so long I used -pg compilation flag and profiled the CPU. The bottleneck was init_SNDATA_EVENT and init_SNLC_ARRAYS, both of which looped over few x 10^4 epochs. The large MXEPOCH is needed for DDF 10 years. After fixing these init loops to only loop over previous NOBS, the read-speed increased significantly to few thousand per second.

The final improvement came from realizing that every event is fully read by the underlying C-code reader, and then the CID-list check is done in the fortran code (snana.exe, snlc_fit.exe). Should run much faster if the C-code reader checks the user CID list and bails from reading the entire event. This logic was added; see variables and functions with CCID_SAVELIST in the name.
With all of the above updates, the read speed is now about 7500/sec on LSST events, or x10 faster than previous. Reading thru 1 million events should now take a little over 2 minutes.

body:
## Summary

`read_searcheff_raw_varnames` (`src/sntools_trigger.c`) hardcodes the filter-split bound to `4`, which is inconsistent with the sibling parser `assign_MAP_VARNAME_FILTERS` in the same file. Any SEARCHEFF_SPEC / SEARCHEFF_zHOST map whose `VARNAMES` combines more than 4 filters with `+`/`-` aborts, even though the map machinery itself supports up to `MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP` (=60).

## Abort message

```
FATAL ERROR ABORT called by read_searcheff_raw_varnames->nsplitString->splitString
  Nsplit = 8  exceeds bound MXsplit=4
  string to split= 'a+b+c+d+e+f+g+h'  ; split separator= '+'
```

## Root cause

Two parsers in `src/sntools_trigger.c` split the map `VARNAMES` on `+`/`-`, but use different bounds:

- `assign_MAP_VARNAME_FILTERS` — **correct**:
  ```c
  int MXSUBSTR = MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP;   // line ~1624  (=60)
  ```
- `read_searcheff_raw_varnames` — **stale literal**:
  ```c
  int MXSUBSTR=4, NSUBSTR, isub ;          // line ~1840
  ```

`read_searcheff_raw_varnames` runs first (as the raw-varname pre-reader), so it aborts before the map parser that would have accepted the same string. The header already documents the intended limit:

```c
// src/sntools_trigger.h:53
#define MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP 60 // e.g., g+r+i+z is max number of + separated substrings
```

Both functions were introduced in the SEARCHEFF refactor (commit `95ff5c0`, 2026-03-27); `MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP` was later raised from 4 → 60 (commit `a9c59b3`, 2026-05-22), but the hardcoded `4` in `read_searcheff_raw_varnames` was missed.

## Proposed fix

`src/sntools_trigger.c`, `read_searcheff_raw_varnames`:

```diff
-  int MXSUBSTR=4, NSUBSTR, isub ;
+  int MXSUBSTR = MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP, NSUBSTR, isub ;
```

Purely enlarges a bound (60 ≥ any realistic filter count), so it is backward-compatible and has no effect on maps combining ≤4 filters.

## How to reproduce

Run `pippin.sh -v JT_TITAN_SPECEFF.yml` from `/project2/rkessler/SURVEYS/ATLAS/USERS/jtweddle/EFFICIENCIES/PIPPIN_FILES`. Abort occurs during map read.

## Context / motivation

ATLAS has 8 (a–h) orange bands to reflect the different CCD+filter combinations across the different telescope units. A single combined-band block `a+b+c+d+e+f+g+h` is the correct way to key the spec-classification efficiency on the source's peak orange mag (the `+` path in `get_searcheff_mag` averages the valid per-chip peak mags). Splitting into 8 separate single-band blocks is not equivalent — they OR-combine and, with `OPT_EXTRAP` on the `−9` sentinels of unobserved chips, silently return eff=1. So the combined block is, I believe, required, and it currently can't be parsed.

comments.body: Fixed. And thank you [Claude?] for chasing down the exact code line of bug
Yep, turns out Claude is very good at this sort of thing! Thanks Rick!

title: `read_searcheff_raw_varnames` hardcodes `MXSUBSTR=4`, ignoring `MXSUBSTR_SEARCHEFF_MAP` — aborts on SPECEFF/zHOST maps combining >4 filters

for bias correcctions (BCOR) in BBC,  fieldlist_biascor is often used to define "IDSAMPLE" subsets to compute independent BCOR. FIeld overlaps give priority to the first field in the list; e.g.
fieldgroup_biascor=DDF,WFD -> overlap priority uses DDF BCOR
fieldgroup_biascor=WFD,DDF -> overlap priority uses WFD BCOR

It may be useful to explicity define a separate BCOR for overlaps, rather than using the priority; however, 
fieldgroup_biascor=WFD,DDF,WFD+DDF
results in abort due to ambiguity.

comments.body:
To define field-overlaps as a separate fieldgroup,
fieldgroup_biascor=WFD,DDF,|WFD+DDF|
where the vertical bars indicate an exclusive fieldgroup that allows only the field overlap, but does not allow WFD or DDF in isolation. Be careful to monitor the overlap BCOR statistics since overlap regions may be small.

I fixed wfit to apply -snrms to MUCOV when reading MUCOV_SYS, and to abort when reading MUCOV_TOT_INV since there is no easy way to update the already-inverted cov matrix.

comments.body:
After discussion, pondering solution: 
1) add ABORT_ON_MISSING_EVENT: 1 to top of header override files to require every event has an entry 
and 
2) add ABORT_ON_NOQZPHOT to allow option to continue if no quantiles are present

realized that ABORT_ON_MISSING_EVENT is anoying because it forces specifying every event in OVERRIDE file, which may include zSPEC (that don't need quantiles) and junk for which we don't want to bother evaluating quantiles. 

A more practical option is to specify
 IGNORE_DATAFILE_VALUE: 1
to instruct SNANA data-reader to NOT read data-FITS columns that are in the OVERRIDE file so that missing events in override will have SNANA-initialized values such as 0 or -9.

Fixed quantile override (sntools_data.c) so that if -9 are specfied for all quantiles, the corresponding HOSTGAL_PHOTOZ[_ERR] are also set to -9; i.e., the original (stale) HOSTGAL_PHOTOZ[ERR] is not preserved if there are no valid quantiles.

While fixing this issue, I stumbled on and fixed another bug. Using IMPLICIT method for quantile overrides (QZPHOT00 ... QZPHOTnn), only igal=0 was loaded; values for igal>0 were getting clobbered.

body:
The original photo-z quantile structure in SNANA data files was to have explicit 
ZPHOT_Q000, ZPHOT_Q010, ZPHOT_Q020 ... ZPHOT_Q100 
columns, and the quantile percentiles were fixed. This rigid structure allowed only 11 quantiles, and worked only for the nearest host. This data structure needs to be more flexible for quantiles, and to allow a new LOGMASS grid so that LOGMASS can be evaluated after the SN+HOST lightcurve fit.

comments.body:
New data stream vectors are

TTYPE62 = 'HOSTGALz_NBIN_QUANTILE_ZPHOT' / label for field  62                  
TTYPE63 = 'HOSTGALz_QUANTILE_ZPHOT' / label for field  63                       
TTYPE64 = 'HOSTGALz_QUANTILE_PERCENT' / label for field  64      
               
TTYPE65 = 'HOSTGALz_NBIN_LOGMASS_ZGRID' / label for field  65                   
TTYPE66 = 'HOSTGALz_LOGMASS_ZGRID' / label for field  66                        
TTYPE67 = 'HOSTGALz_LOGMASS_VALGRID' / label for field  67                      
TTYPE68 = 'HOSTGALz_LOGMASS_ERRGRID' / label for field  68     

TTYPE105= 'HOSTGAL2z_NBIN_QUANTILE_ZPHOT' / label for field 105                 
TTYPE106= 'HOSTGAL2z_QUANTILE_ZPHOT' / label for field 106                      
TTYPE107= 'HOSTGAL2z_QUANTILE_PERCENT' / label for field 107       
             
TTYPE108= 'HOSTGAL2z_NBIN_LOGMASS_ZGRID' / label for field 108                  
TTYPE109= 'HOSTGAL2z_LOGMASS_ZGRID' / label for field 109                       
TTYPE110= 'HOSTGAL2z_LOGMASS_VALGRID' / label for field 110                     
TTYPE111= 'HOSTGAL2z_LOGMASS_ERRGRID' / label for field 111

there is a new caveat reading these vectors with python. While reading FITS data into astropy table works fine, table.to_pandas() fails on the vector columns, which caused scone to fail. The scone fix in $SCONE_DIR/create_heatmaps/helpers.py was to add a new function, remove_vector_columns(table), that removes vector columns before converting to pandas. Perhaps a more simple one-liner can be identified later.

LEGACY COLUMN NAMES: 

for the HOSTLIB read by simulation, the legacy columns HOSTGAL_ZPHOT_Q000 ... HOSTGAL_ZPHOT_Q100 are still allowed, but recommend replacing with the more flexible QZPHOT00 ... QZPHOTnn column names.

OVERRIDE files (read by snana.exe and snlc_fit.exe)  IMPLICIT z-list must use QZPHOT00, QZPHOT01 ... QZPHOTnn, where PERCENTILES are computed with implicit assumption about equal-spaced quantile probs. If legacy HOSTGAL_ZPHOT_Qnn are detected, the code aborts with instructions to use the QZPHOT column names.

In short, old notation still allowed for HOSTLIB_FILE, but not for HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE

OPT_PHOTOZ += 32768 (internally convert Gauss PDF into quantiles) is broken, and needs to be fixed later (or removed). Follow USE_QGAUSS logical in sntools_host.c. This is a feature only for debugging, so not critical.
released with REFAC_DATA_FLAG=1 ... no going back.

Few years ago we corrected the PV implementation to be such as:
```
    IF ( DOCOR_VPEC ) THEN

       ZPEC     = ( SNLC_VPEC     / SNGL(CLIGHT) )
       ZPECERR  = ( SNLC_VPEC_ERR / SNGL(CLIGHT) )

       if ( RESTORE_WRONG_VPEC ) then

          SNLC_ZHD = (1.0+SNLC_ZCMB) * (1.0+ZPEC) - 1.0  ! Jan 2018;
       else

          SNLC_ZHD = (1.0+SNLC_ZCMB) / (1.0+ZPEC) - 1.0  ! Oct 2020
       endif

       ZERR1 = SNLC_ZCMB_ERR
       ZERR2 = ZPECERR * (1.0 + SNLC_ZCMB) ! Eq A1, Davis 2012
       SNLC_ZHD_ERR = sqrt(ZERR1*ZERR1 + ZERR2*ZERR2)
    ENDIF

body:
In the snlc_fit.exe program, the use of HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE in the fit-input file has become more complicated (i.e, long comma-sep lists) in the Pantheon+ and DES-SN5YR analyses. The overrides include redshifts, vpec, host properties, and future analyses will include photo-z (mean, stdev, quantiles) and maybe even mag corrections (e.g., chromatic corr and bug fixes from a DR). Implementing override changes and systematics is tricky and subject to mistakes because sometimes an override file is added to a list, and sometimes a systematic override file replaces an already existing override file.

As we move to Roman and Rubin, where data releases are controlled by the project, the use of HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE is likely to become even more prevalent and complex. To simplify management of the override system, here is a proposal to define OVERRIDE folders, analogous to data folders, rather than explicit lists. For example, the fit-input file could look something like

&SNLCINP
    VERSION_PHOTOMETRY = 'SURVEY_DR2'
    OVERRIDE_DIR                  = '/PATH/SURVEY_OVR_NOMINAL'

and for systematics
    FITOPT:  
    - /SYS_VPEC/     OVERRIDE_DIR   '/PATH/SURVEY_OVR_SYS_VPEC'
    - /SYS_ZPHOT/  OVERRIDE_DIR   '/PATH/SURVEY_OVR_SYS_ZPHOT'
    etc ...

Analogous to the VERSION_PHOTOMETY folder, OVERRIDE_DIR is a folder containing a list file using the base name of the folder.
SURVEY_OVR_SYS_VPEC.LIST      # list of HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE
The snlc_fit.exe program would simply read the list and construct the comma-sep list internally. 

An optional MAGCOR.DAT file in the same folder can specify epoch-dependent mag-corrections (see snana manual:  5.28.4 Epoch-Dependent Mag Corrections).

The goal of this system is to simplify:
* organization and provenance-tracking of HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILEs
* implementation of NOMINAL and systematic OVERRIDEs within a collaboration
* updating data files to include NOMINAL overrides (e..g, internal or public DR)

Another subtle point is that systematics with OVERRIDEs are not identical for data and sim in the way that changing a cut is identical. The problem is that data and sim have different CIDs. To handle data and sims, the top-level list file could be a YML file with

OVERRIDE_FILE_DATA:
   --  <override1.dat>
   --  <override2.dat>
   --  <override3.dat>

OVERRIDE_FILE_SIM:
   -- etc ...

comments.body: Based on comments in DES-SN5YR zHOST map, ad-hoc color cannot be defined in the zHOST map, and explicit JH_color would need to be explicitly added to HOSTLIB. To avoid such hacks in the future, I will work on allowing ad-hoc colors in the zHOST map, hopefully able to use the SPEC_FILE map tools that allow ad-hoc color for spec-efficiency map.

The underlying problem is that the SPEC and zHOST map codes are mostly independent and they do not share attributes. For example SPEC_FILE map can define colors, but zHOST cannot; zHOST map can use only HOSTLIB variables while SPEC map canot use HOSTLIB variables.

The fix requires a semi-major refactor in two parts:
1. in sntools_trigger.c[h],  merge SPEC and zHOST-map code into a single code operating on a well defined SEARCHEFF_MAP_DEF object, and 
2. in sntools_host.c[h], read HOSTLIB variables before checking SPEC,zHOST,GENPDF map variables; split old read_head_HOSTLIB() into two parts, read_head_HOSTLIB and prep_head_HOSTLIB().

Refactor code is ready using

body:
In BBC/SALT2mu.exe, the biasCor is applied separately to each IDSAMPLE (e.g., shallow vs. deep) defined by the user. IDSAMPLE is based on survey and field, and is ordered in a reproducible way, regardless of order in data file, so that each IDSAMPLE has the same meaning for data and sim. However, it was recently noticed that for zSPEC/zPHOT mixture, the ordering depends on the data set order, and can thus be different for data and sim.
Here is an example for DES:

  IDSAMPLE= 0 --> DES-zSPEC(X3)         (NDATA   =   562, 0.017<z<1.227)
  IDSAMPLE= 1 --> DES-zPHOT(X3)         (NDATA   =   372, 0.038<z<1.183)
  IDSAMPLE= 2 --> DES-zPHOT(C3)         (NDATA   =   418, 0.063<z<1.195)
  IDSAMPLE= 3 --> DES-zSPEC(C3)         (NDATA   =   555, 0.066<z<1.226)
  IDSAMPLE= 4 --> DES-zPHOT(X1+X2)      (NDATA   =   221, 0.009<z<1.132)
  IDSAMPLE= 5 --> DES-zSPEC(X1+X2)      (NDATA   =   649, 0.033<z<1.160)
  IDSAMPLE= 6 --> DES-zSPEC(S1+S2)      (NDATA   =   579, 0.051<z<1.195)
  IDSAMPLE= 7 --> DES-zPHOT(S1+S2)      (NDATA   =   226, 0.023<z<1.161)
  IDSAMPLE= 8 --> DES-zSPEC(E1+E2+C1+C  (NDATA   =  1275, 0.044<z<1.226)
  IDSAMPLE= 9 --> DES-zPHOT(E1+E2+C1+C  (NDATA   =   488, 0.009<z<1.189)

While the FIELDs are ordered correctly based on the fieldGroup input key, zSPEC and zPHOT order for each FIELD-group is essentially random.

comments.body:
In SALT2mu.c,  see new internal variable REFAC_SORT_IDSAMPLE=0 by default, and enabled by input debug_flag=212; thus legacy behavior is still default. 

The strategy in sort_IDSAMPLE_biasCor is to call it twice with 'zSPEC' and 'zPHOT' args to sort each half separately; the sorting works,

  IDSAMPLE= 0 --> DES-zSPEC(X3)         (NDATA   =   562, 0.017<z<1.227)
  IDSAMPLE= 1 --> DES-zSPEC(C3)         (NDATA   =   555, 0.066<z<1.226)
  IDSAMPLE= 2 --> DES-zSPEC(X1+X2)      (NDATA   =   649, 0.033<z<1.160)

  IDSAMPLE= 4 --> DES-zSPEC(E1+E2+C1+C  (NDATA   =  1275, 0.044<z<1.226)
  IDSAMPLE= 5 --> DES-zPHOT(X3)         (NDATA   =   372, 0.038<z<1.183)

body:
This issue is a follow-up to https://github.com/RickKessler/SNANA/issues/1605, where the wfit C code crashes when reading covtot_inv_000.npz on Perlmutter that had been recently updated to python v3.12 (was 3.11 before). Jonah noted that 'allowe_pickle' key was missing, so he wrote a hack script to read the npz file, restore the missing 'allowe_pickle'  key, and re-write the npz files; wfit works with re-written npz files. 

After more investigation, the allowe_pickle key has nothing to do with this problem, but Jonah had accidentally re-written the npz file without compression (np.savez instead of np.savez_compressed in original create_covariance code).

The implicit assumption here is that the cnpy (C-code) library can no longer handle npz compression with python v3.12, or numpy 2.2.6 that may have been recently updated as well. 

Tests on HD with ~1000 entries show that the uncompressed npz file size is only a few percent bigger than compressed files ... as long as all of the covtot entries are filled. For the NOSYS cov that has only diagonal elements, the uncompressed file is the same size as COV with all elements, in contrast to the compressed NOSYS file that is much smaller due to compression of the redundant zeros. Gzipping the uncompressed NOSYS cov file results in a much smaller file size, but it cannot be read with C code (wfit) without unzipping it.

comments.body: create_covariance has been modified with np.savez_compressed replaced with np.savez. An AI search indicates that cpny++ can handle compressed npz files, but I will postpone such an update until later if/when there is a need to compress NOSYS cov files. Another option is to add a cov_flag (= 'cov' or 'diag') to the npz file; for the latter it would write only the diagonal elements in a 1D array.

body:
Within the BBC class of submit_batch_jobs, the logic of naming output dirs was as follows:

1. if there are multiple input data sets (e.g., LOWZ + DES), then the output dirs have generic names OUTPUT_BBCFIT-[datasetnumber] 
2. if there is only one data set, the output dir name is the name of the data version 

While there is no explicit bug or problem here, the problem occurs when pippin is used and there is only one data set (e.g., DES only). Pippin assumes the generic folder names with OUTPUT_BBCFIT, but for a single data set the folder name is incorrect and all stage 8 (wfit) tasks fail.

Indeed this is the classic case of "it's a feature, not a bug"

comments.body: The fix here is rather simple: remove the the logic in bullet 2 above, and always use the same logic and OUTPUT_BBCFIT naming.

In the process of searching this issue in the code, I noticed a feature from April 1 2025 using devel_flag=41 had never been made default. This feature allows combining 1 LOWZ data set with multiple HIGH-Z data sets (and vice-versa) to enable studies in which one of the sub-sets is exactly the same. The devel_flag=41 logic has been removed, bbc_prep_1version_match_legacy() is removed, and bbc_prep_1version_match() is now called to implement the 4.01.2025 feature.
verified with pippin.

if zero events are written from a snlc_sim.exe task (NGENLC_WRITE=0), the output README key GENTYPE_TO_NAME is blank because the relevant information is obtained from events passing trigger. For sims with very low stats, some of the SPLIT tasks have zero events and others have a few. The sim-merge process checks only the first README file (out of the N_CORE readme files) and checks for GENTYPE_TO_NAME, which can be blank if by random chance the first README has NGENLC_WRITE=0.

This is a fairly harmless feature, except when SCONE tries to read this sim-readme key and finds insufficient information, resulting in a crash.

comments.body:
Two fixes have been implemented.
1. a less robust fix in snlc_sim.c to generate GENTYPE_TO_NAME information after events are generated, rather than after passing trigger. However, if an event is not generated (e.g., MJD range has no overlap with SIMLIB cadence), this fix still results in blank GENTYPE_TO_NAME in the README file


2. a more robust fix in submit_prog_sim.py to loop thru the set of README files (instead of using only the first one), and picking the first README with NGENLC_WRITE > 0.

Created new util  ../util/convert_snana_f77_to_f90.py,
and this script has been used this to create
   snana.F90
   snlc_fit.F90
   psnid.F90

Makefile works the same way with the same gfortran calls. Only change is to suppress the ypatchy call in the Makefile. 


Use of *.F90 files begins with snana code version v12_00

A nice feature of this language switch is that code can run outside the 6-80 column limit of F77.

Found and fixed subtle bug from f77 -> f90 switch. In F77, some of the table variable init calls (ADDCOL) assume common block memory alignment for things like RA,DEC or zHD,zHDERR ... but in F90 there are no common blocks and the alignment assumption results in corrupted table values. The fix is to split the compact  ADDCOL (... "RA,DEC") into two separate calls for RA and DEC, respectively. Note that memory alignment with arrays (e.g., SNRMAX(5)) still works.

comments.body: I look at few LC of cutted SN Ia but didn't notice something special. Here is an example: The vertical line represent the estimated PEAKMJD from snlc_fit.exe

The paradox is due to different definitions of CUTWIN_TRESTMIN[MAX] in the sim and in the analysis code (likely an accident  in the distant past). The simulation cut is on any epoch, but the snlc_fit analysis cut is on the extreme min or max within CUTWIN_TREST. With your current cuts,

 CUTWIN_TREST     = -20.0,   60.0
  cutwin_Trestmin  = -10.0   0.
   cutwin_Trestmax  =  0.   30.

if there is an observation with TREST between -20 and -10, it will fail the cut. Similarly, a TREST observation between 30 and 60 fails cut. The intended usage here is
cutwin_Trestmin  = -20.0   0
cutwin_Trestmax  =  0.   60.

which recovers all the events.
I would recommend NOT using CUTWIN in the simulation because it does not always map into analysis cuts. Sim CUTS use truth, for example, not measured values. I have even thought about removing the CUTWIN feature in the sim.

To do what you want, we could add something like
    SNCUT_NOBS_TREST = '1 -10 0 : 2 0 30'
meaning at least 1 obs from -10 to 0, and at least 2 obs from 0 to 30.

Thanks for the explanation!

I agree for SIM cuts, it's better if they are agnostic to infered parameters! 

I think the feature you propose will be super useful !
Follow development of new  SNCUT_NOBS_TREST in https://github.com/RickKessler/SNANA/issues/1588

body:
I am interested in the positions of supernovae in my Pilot HLTDS simulations. I ran two different versions: one in which the RA/DECs are taken exactly from the SIMLIB, resulting in multiple SNe with identical RA/DECs; and one in which I use the SNANA key MXRADIUS_RANDOM_SHIFT: 0.01, which is supposed to randomly shift RA/DECs to within the given radius (in my case 0.01 arcsec). This shift seems arbitrary; what is a good rule of thumb for which value I should use for this key? 

My output on Midway without the shift: $PIPPIN_OUTPUT/JP_1TEMPLATE_7VISIT_115BUDGET_NOINTERLACE
My output on Midway WITH the shift: $PIPPIN_OUTPUT/JP_1TEMPLATE_7VISIT_115BUDGET_NOINTERLACE_RADEC

comments.body:
First of all, from the manual we have
   MXRADIUS_RANDOM_SHIFT: 0.01  # circle radius, degrees
so the unit is degrees, not arc seconds. 
There is no rule of thumb here since it is a rarely used feature.
Based on size of SIMLIB and area covered, you can compute the average distance between SIMLIB entries, so it would make sense to set MXRADIUS_RANDOM_SHIFT to something like half the mean separation.

SIMLIB was missing NLIBID key and thus simulation could not determine random start locations for each core; this resulted in using the same LIBIDs (hence RA, DEC) for each core. To prevent future confusion, snlc_sim has been modified to abort if NLIBID key is missing for batch mode.

body:
Hi,

Running a Rubin-LSST simulation on NERSC with @erikpeterson23  we found an excess of generated supernovae.
We are simulating 10 years of Rubin-LSST with two different simulations for "low-z" (0 <  z < 0.11) and "high-z" (0.11 < z < 1.3). For the high-z sample, we are finding, after fit cuts, ~ 1.5 million SNe Ia, which seems overestimated.

The cadence file is : `$SNANA_LSST_ROOT/simlibs/baseline_v4.3_10yrs_all.SIMLIB.COADD`
With survey parameters:
```
SOLID_ANGLE: 6.225
TOTAL_AREA: 20434.964
DNDZ: POWERLAW 2.06E-5 1.7 # Frohmaier 2019 rescale to h = 0.6774
```
The simulation is distributed over 10 CPUs using:

```
    NGEN_UNIT: 0.1
    RANSEED_REPEAT: 10 17234
    BATCH_INFO: sbatch $SBATCH_TEMPLATES/SBATCH_DEFAULT.TEMPLATE 20
```

We are applying SEARCHEFF detection cut using:
```
SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_EFF_FILE: $SNANA_LSST_ROOT/models/searcheff/SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_LSST_DC2_Run2.2i_WFD.DAT
SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_LOGIC_FILE: $SNANA_LSST_ROOT/models/searcheff/SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_LOGIC_DC2_Run2.2i_WFD.DAT
```

The overall PIPPIN configuration is given in: `$PIPPIN_OUTPUT/EP-LSST/EP-LSST.yml`

comments.body:
From Phil Gris work, we expect about 20,000 SNIa after cuts in DDF (e.g., see Fig 1 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.10781) that spans 50 deg sq. Guessing that the WFD will have 1/5 the number of SN per sq deg results in 4,000 per 50 deg sq. Over half the sky we naively expect
   N(WFD) ~ 20,000(DDF) * (1/5) * (20,000/50) = 1.6 million
which is pretty close to what you find above.

In [Gris et al. 2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4365/ac9e58/pdf) it is stated:

> In a recent paper (Lochner et al. 2022), the LSST Dark
Energy Science Collaboration (DESC) has presented an
analysis from the WFD survey observing strategies simulated
by the LSST project. 12 The conclusion is that an unprecedented
number of well-measured SNe Ia will be observed in the WFD
survey (between 120,000 and 170,000) up to redshifts z ∼ 0.3.

Do you think there is an error in this statement? or am I mis-understanding something?

Also DDF is going deeper: if we said that DDF is complete up to `z~1.1` and WFD is complete up to `z~0.5` it gives an extra 0.15 factor in term of volume ratio. Thus the volume of WFD is N(WFD) = 20,000(DDF) * (1/5) * (20,000/50)  * 0.15  ~  240 000 SNe Ia
Did you use the same cuts as in Lochner 2022 (4th paragraph in Sec 5)? They are rather harsh cuts compared to current analyses with real data.

Yes the 200k estimation is based on these cuts, the cut in the simulation are less stringent... This is true that the visits requirements in Lochner 2022 are high, but is it enough to explain the ~80 ratio of SNe Ia? maybe we should just input the same cuts in SNANA to see ?

Recent Roman studies show that this results in truncated (but harmless) chi2grid maps that can cause confusion, and introduces a small (<0.01) bias in w0 and wa.

Added a new input parameter -speed_nsig_multiplier with default = 15 (instead of 6).
To check speed degradation, here is a test using different nsig values on Roman UNBINNED HD  from arXiv:2506.04402:

nsig06.log:	 Elapsed time =  39776  secfor: chi2 bin   242757 of   242757
nsig10.log:	 Elapsed time =  44682  sec for: chi2 bin   242757 of   242757
nsig15.log:	 Elapsed time =  50543  sec for: chi2 bin   242757 of   242757
nsig9999.log: Elapsed time =  61969  sec for: chi2 bin   242757 of   242757


The last test with nsig999 removes this speed trick completely.
Increasing nsig = 6 --> 15 increases CPU time by factor of 1.27, but is still a factor of 1.22 faster than no speed trick. Users can set  -speed_nsig_multiplier to smaller values to obtain faster fitting speed, with the above-mentioned caveats in performance.

Recent pippin job with photometric sample using BAYESN results in LCFIT abort because Y-band at lower redshifts is not valid:

  - FATAL ERROR ABORT called by genmag_BAYESN->checkLamRange_SEDMODEL 
  - LSST-Y lambda range is outside defined SED range. 
  - Consider using &FITINP variable RESTLAMBDA_FITRANGE. 
  

(On Perlmutter, see $PIPPIN_OUTPUT/CBAYESN_ANALYSIS/2_LCFIT/FIT_DATA_LSST_LSST_SIMDATA)

comments.body:
I traced this abort to a non-SNIa event that has a broader wavelength range compared to BayeSN. The sim code protects SNIa-BAYESN, but doesn't protect non-IA because it doesn't know that BAYESN will be used later at LCFIT stage. The problem is here in the BAYESN.YAML file:

L_FILTER_CEN_MIN: 4500
L_FILTER_CEN_MAX: 8500   <=== too close to SED upper bound of 9500
L_SED_MIN: 3500
L_SED_MAX: 9500

The central wavelength limit of 8500 is too close to the max SED range of 9500, and Y-band centered at 8500 can still leak out of the SED range.

This problem would eventually fail on real data that records all bands regardless of redshift, and it indeed fails on ELASTICC SNIa that records all bands regardless of redshift or rest-frame wavelength. I setup an elastic test job here,

$PIPPIN_OUTPUT/CBAYESN_ANALYSIS/2_LCFIT/FIT_DATA_LSST_LSST_SIMDATA/output/SPLIT_JOBS_LCFIT/rick_elasticc.sh

that ABORTS rather quickly, so I would suggest tuning L_FILTER_CEN_MAX until LCFIT-BAYESN can process ELASTICC Ia without the wavelength range ABORT
temp solution is to artificially extend phase and wavelength range in existing BAYESN models; longer term plan is to improve training to include wider phase range.

body:
The SNANA zeropoint of 27.5 is a strange artifact of early (pre-SNANA) development with SDSS data in the 2000s. In slow the process of learning astronomy, I picked an arbitrary flux scale of E+11 so that calibrated SDSS fluxes roughly corresponded to photo-electrons. For unknown reasons, this scale (ZP=27.5) stuck when SNANA was later developed and became public. 

It is now long overdue to switch this ZP to 31.4, corresponding to nJy, but maintain back-compatibility.

The first step is to add ZP_FLUXCAL into data headers, both TEXT and FITS. Analysis codes should use this value to convert Synthetic MAG -> FLUXCAL and vice-versa. If ZP_FLUXCAL is missing in a data header, the codes should automatically fall back to the legacy 27.5 value so that older data folders can be processed.

Next, define ZP_FLUXCAL input for the simulation. This input is to allow testing both ZP values before making the big switch, and is not intended for users.

The default zero point is now defined in sndata.h as follows:

#define ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_SNANA_ORIG  27.5
#define ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_nJy         31.4
#define ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_DEFAULT    ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_SNANA_ORIG

To make the final switch (at later time TBD), replace the last line with
#define ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_DEFAULT   ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL_nJy

The main warning in this new system will be that new data sets should include ZP_FLUXCAL key, otherwise SNANA's snlc_fit.exe will automatically assume that ZP=27.5, even if your new FLUXCAL values use ZP=31.4. I had thought about using data file time stamps to determine if older ZP=27.5 should be used, but this would break if older data folders are copied instead of moved.
title: Change SNANA ZEROPOINT_FLUXCAL from 27.5 to 31.4 (nJy)

I am experiencing `wfit.exe` returning `w = -1` when using dummy data to generate Hubble diagrams as part of learning how `wfit.exe` works.

All files are located in:

$SNANA_DEBUG/myc21_wfit

---

### Context

This is part of **Problem 4(e)** of the SNANA tutorial, where we test recovery of cosmological parameters  \$w$ and \$\Omega_M$.

I simulate an ideal redshift-binned Hubble diagram with:

Redshifts: 0.05, 0.15, …, 0.95
True parameters: ΩM = 0.3, ΩDE = 0.7, w = -1

---

###  Python Code Used

```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.cosmology import FlatwCDM

z_vals = np.array([0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95])
cosmo = FlatwCDM(H0=70, Om0=0.3, w0=-1.0)  # or w0 = -2.0 for testing
mu_vals = cosmo.distmod(z_vals).value
sigma_mu = 0.1 * np.ones_like(mu_vals)

with open("myc21_my_hd.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("VARNAMES: CID zHD MU MUERR\n")
    for i, (z, mu, sig) in enumerate(zip(z_vals, mu_vals, sigma_mu)):
        cid = f"SN_{i+1:04d}"
        f.write(f"{cid} {z:.3f} {mu:.3f} {sig:.3f}\n")
```

---

### How I Run wfit:

wfit.exe myc21_my_hd.txt

--- 

### Problem

When I simulate a Hubble diagram using w = -2, the wfit.exe output still returns w = -1. This suggests that the input file may not be processed correctly, yet there is no error or warning to indicate an issue. Initially, I observed that I was consistently getting w = -1 from wfit.exe regardless of the Hubble diagram I provided. To test whether the code was responsive to input changes, I intentionally generated mock data with a clearly different w value (e.g., w = -2) — but the output remained unchanged. This silent behavior makes it difficult to diagnose formatting or content issues during exploratory testing.

--- 

### Request

Would you mind taking a look at my Hubble diagrams and output files in $SNANA_DEBUG/myc21_wfit? I’d appreciate it if you could help find the mistake on my end.

fits for wCDM model. To fit w0waCDM,

Hi Rick,

I am experiencing some inconsistencies with scatter in my simulated data that I am finding difficult to explain.

I have calibrated my simulations such that the simulated flux errors and SNR very closely match the data, as you can see from the below plots.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7d34e507-b6bc-46ec-8ac9-34999725beda)
Ratio of simulated to real flux errors as function of real AB magnitude

Ratio of simulated to real SNR as function of real SNR

Given that the flux errors align, I would expect that the simulated scatter would align with the data as well. However when I look at the flux pull (defined as ```(flux-weighted_mean_flux)/flux_err``` where the weighted mean flux is computed intranight, which for ATLAS typically contains 4 exposures), I find that this is centred at zero with a standard deviation of 0.9, rather than the expected standard deviation of 1 as we see for the data (see below).

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d39b9126-90ff-4357-8093-ff91322d2c40)
Flux pull distribution of simulated data

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0bef5ee6-17c1-40c9-a656-6d31accbf838)
Flux pull distribution for real data

Is there something that SNANA is doing internally to alter the scatter by ~10% without altering the flux uncertainties? I see something along these lines in §4.14 of the manual, but given that I am not supplying any sort of flux error map/model I suppose this would only occur if a default map is applied in the absence of one being specified?

The sim input file I am using is located at `/project2/rkessler/SURVEYS/ATLAS/USERS/jtweddle/EFFICIENCIES/CALIBRATE/sim_input_atlas.input`, in case there is something in there that I am not using correctly.

Thanks again for your help!
Jack

body:
Example: 80 cores submitted for 25 sim-data sets, each with 20 systematics, and the same-event sync option is set. Nominal analysis FITOPT000 must finish first before any FITOPTs are processed. If the system only allocates 20 cores at a time, the jobs will never finish because all 80 FITOPT000 contributions must complete before any task moves onto FITOPT001.

Need smarter logic where each data set is processed by only a few cores, and not dependent on all 80 cores running.

comments.body:
Done.
In above example, submit_batch_jobs  uses int(80/25) = 3 cores per data set, or 75 cores total ... hence 5 of the 80 requested cores are not used.
The first 3 CPU*CMD files process all of data set 1; the next 3 CPU*.CMD files process all of data set 2, etc ...

A relative quick 1/2 hour test shows that even with 10% fewer cores, overall wall time is still 10% less, likely due to much less overhead running jobs and merging because the total number of jobs is about x10 smaller with this new logic. If many cores have long wait times, the wall time improvement should be even greater.

title: submit_batch_jobs: Need smarter logic for distributing LCFIT jobs with systematics

I introduced a nasty memory leak in a refactor last week; should be fixed now.
The original issue (last week) was that FITS files were closed before opening next FITS file ... which meant that last FITS file was never closed. This works fine if only one data version is processed, but causes a crash if multiple data versions are processed. The recent refactor is to ensure that last FITS file is always closed. The tricky part is that last event is not necessarily read for batch jobs because only 1 of NCORE events are read, so figuring out when to close a FITS file is not so obvious. 

Today's fix keeps old logic of closing FITS file just before opening a new file ... and new logic that closes last FITS file when VERSION-DONE flag is passed after reading entire data version.

body:
Managing duplicate CIDs in SNANA codes is based on the assumption that "CID_IDSURVEY" is unique, but this is not sufficient if the same SURVEY is simulated separately with different fields; e.g LSST-WFD (for low-z) and LSST-DDF. All is fine if WFD and DDF are simulated together in the same submit_batch_jobs because unique CIDs are garanteed for all events. However, if WFD and DDF are generated with two distinct  launches of  submit_batch_jobs, there can be random CID overlaps with the same IDSURVEY. 

The fix is to match events based on "CID_IDSURVEY_FIELD".

body: Sometimes BBC fit gets crazy errors (too small or too large for distances). While BBC code reports this problem in the stdout and in the output YAML file, submit_batch_jobs (and hence pippin) do not read this error and the pipeline just carries on with this crazy output.

comments.body: Also found a bad crazy error trap in BBC/SALT2mu for BS21 dust model. Original crazy-error is based on assuming sigint ~ 0.1 mag ... but for dust model, very blue events have smaller distance error and thus BBC sometimes reports false crazy error warnings.

Inside SALT2mu.c code, min-M0err trap is scaled by average sqrt(muCOVscale) in the redshift bin, to avoid false alarms.

Previously only 1 repeat fit was allowed ... updated to allow up to two repeat fits (3 total).  End of STDOUT and YAML file include total number of fits: NFIT_EXEC. Usually NFIT_EXEC=1, but NFIT_EXEC>1 if crazy M0-errors are detected and the fit is repeated.

If there are crazy errors after SALT2mu/BBC fit, it writes
BAD_OUTPUT:  True

to output YAML file, and submit_batch_jobs reads BAD_OUTPUT and flags error and writes FAIL inside ALL.DONE --> pippin will stop.

title: fix submit_batch_jobs to trap BBC fit error and post FAIL to ALL.DONE

For small systematic shifts in snlc_fit (SALT light curve fit), the resulting fit parameters sometimes change a lot, which is not physical and results in a much larger MU error that deweights these events on the Hubble diagram. This effect is NOT captured in BBC. As an example, consider a photo-z fit with a systematic shift that results in adding or dropping a band w.r.t. nominal fit ... the resulting fit-par differences can be significant.

To remove these crazy systematics outliers:
1. add option to use nominal (FITOPT000) fit parameters and errors as a Gaussian prior, and 
2. write BANDS to FITRES file, and add option to force using same bands

There are two issues with your spectra being truncated. First, when using TAKE_SPECTRUM keys in the SIMLIB file, the output spectrum is constrained to be within the wavelengths provided in the SNR_LAMOBS key. The reasoning is that the sim should only generate within the wave range of the actual data that these TAKE_SPECTRUM keys represent. It doesn't make sense to simulate & analyze spectra that extend in wavelength beyond actual data. Beyond the first issue, there is additional wavelength truncation due to invalid ZP_SPECTROGRAPH calculation (see manual screen shot below). The current sim code rejects wave bins with ZP<0 (i.e., "invalid"), but does not give any warning, which can result in wave bins mysteriously not appearing in the output spectra. For your spectrograph, about 1/3 of the wave bins have invalid ZP_SPECTROGRAPH < 0, and this is because of the values in MAGREF_LIST: 17.0 32.0 The bright end of 17 is fine, but the faint end of 32 is far too faint, resulting in a poor estimate of ZP. Would suggest increasing the faint end to be closer to the faint end of SN that pass your selection criteria. To avoid future confusion, I added a diagnostic to print ZP(min, max) and to abort if more than 2% of the wave bins fail the ZP>0 cut. Your test job now aborts with this error: FATAL ERROR ABORT called by INIT_SPECTROGRAPH_SEDMODEL Invalid ZP_SPECTROGRAPH frac = 0.335; exceeds FRAC_ZP_INVALID_ABORT=0.020 Check MAGREF_LIST in spectrograph table I checked this diagnostic on the Roman PRISM, and ZPmin/max is about 10-11, well above the ZP>0 requirement. body:
I recently ran this script on a sample with 19k events and 30 systematics, and had to request 128GB of memory, which limits the number of simultaneous jobs allowed by RCC. Most of the memory seems to be wasted on storing each individual sub-matrix of 30 systematics:
   	     30 x 19k^2 x 8 = 86.6 GB. 
To reduce memory consumption, a refactor is needed to keep a running sum of COVSYS_TOT and release the memory for each systematic.

As a side note, recall that create_cov also inverts COVTOT to save time at cosmology fitting stage. The matrix invert time for this 19k^2 matrix was about 5 hr, consistent with O(n^3) number of operations needed to invert.  If we want to invert 100k^2 matrix someday in the future, the CPU time increase is expected to be 5^3 = 125 --> 5 x 125 = 625 hr.  Even using a newer CPU running x10 faster, the CPU time would be a few days and I am not aware of a cluster allowing few-day run time in slurm queue.

comments.body: refactor to save memory by computing and deleting cov matrix contributions on-the-fly. Same	for cov inverse. See internal global FLAG_REDUCE_MEMORY. Also noticed that performing "positive definite" test takes much longer than matrix inversion, so this test now runs only for size < 2000. The comments above about long matrix inversion were really for the pos-def and "condition" test.

body:
This is more a to-do/wishlist, following on from #1431. Over the past few months we've made some improvements to the dust laws implemented in SNANA. There are still some things that could be improved further, listed below:
- [ ] Re-visit the F99-like dust laws depending on the outcome of https://github.com/karllark/dust_extinction/issues/243.
- [x] Make sure all $R_V$ and $\lambda$ limits are enforced properly.
- [x] Possibly implement the second derivatives in the F99 function directly. Currently I have hardcoded some matrices to handle this. It was okay when it was just F99, but now there are three F99-like laws with slightly different arrangements of spline knots, things have really gotten out of hand.
- [x] Add the option to modify the $f_A$ parameter in the [Gordon et al. (2016](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...826..104G/abstract) dust law. I'll need help from @RickKessler with this. Would also be useful to have input from @djbrout about what your intended use case was? (see also #1434)
- [x] Implement additional $R_V$-dependent extinction laws, to "complete the set" of curves from [`dust_extinction`](https://github.com/karllark/dust_extinction). Outstanding ones are listed below.
- [x] Document these things somewhere (done in #1433).

More dust laws to add:
- [x] [Maíz Apellániz et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014A%26A...564A..63M/abstract): This uses a spline, but not quite the same type as F99 (as far as I can tell). They give IDL code in the paper, and an implementation is included in `dust_extinction`. Only optical and NIR (no UV).
- [x] [Fitzpatrick et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...886..108F/abstract): The implementation in `dust_extinction` is based on a B-spline (but that might just be another boundary conditions issue). The paper talks about cubic splines though, and based on past codes Fitzpatrick seems like a natural cubic kinda guy (a man after my own heart). In any case, TBC whether this will be easy or annoying (done in #1437 ).
- [x] [Goobar (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008ApJ...686L.103G/abstract): Power law for circumstellar dust.

comments.body: Cc @ado8, who is thinking about these things in a BayeSN context

The current default version of the Fitzpatrick dust law contains artefacts, and the approximation it is based on breaks down for $R_V\neq 3.1$.

It is based on a polynomial in $\lambda$ that was fit to the ratio of the Fitzpatrick (1999) and O'Donnell (1994) extinction laws. This only approximates the Fitzpatrick (1999) dust law well for $R_V=3.1$, meaning it works for correcting MW extinction, but not as a host-galaxy dust law with arbitrary $R_V$.
title: Fitzpatrick '99 Approximation

this is a subtle gzip bug that I have never been able to fix. When reading a gzip file, rewind causes a rare corruption and thus rewind is not used for gzip files. Even closing and re-opening the gzip file can cause corruption. For GENPDF_FILE, the snana_open command searches for DOCUMENTATION block on first line, but doesn't find it because VARNAMES is on the first line in this particular gzipped GENPDF_FILE. Without the rewind, the remainder of the read-code does not find the first VARNAMES that was already ready while looking for the DOCUMENTATION key.

The simple solution here is to gunzip the GENPDF_FILE (which I did), and the code goes past the previous abort. A more robust solution is to add a DOCUMENTATION block at the top of the file.

comments.body:
The main issue is that there is no sim-input file (above) and thus snlc_sim interprets the SIMLIB file as a sim input file, and the abort is thus correct.

To simplify implementation of SIMLIB_DUMP, there are two code updates:

1) sim-input file need contain only the SIMLIB_FILE keys other required keys (GENMODEL, KCOR_FILE, GENFILTERS) are not needed

2) replacing sim-input file with NOFILE, a command-line only argument can be used for the dump ; e.g.
  snlc_sim.exe NOFILE   SIMLIB_FILE $SNANA_LSST_ROOT/simlibs/LSST_DC2_Run2.2i_WFD.SIMLIB \. SIMLIB_DUMP 1

The SIMLIB_DUMP section of the SNANA manual has been updated accordingly.

body:
after create_covariance.py reads BBC output HD, the data frame is internally sorted by CID, which can cause problems with duplicates in sim data; e.g. independent generation of SNIa and SNCC can have random duplicate CIDs. Sorting by CID results in random ordering among duplicate CIDs, and thus the systematics HDs may be slightly mis-aligned. I noticed this artifact from a crazy wfit-chi2 using HDIBC method that interpolates two HDs. However, this artifact may have impacted previous simulated data samples that processed with systematics.

This bug should not impact data provided that there are no duplicates.

comments.body:
The fix is to sort by redshift and CID;
replace
   df = df.sort_values([ "CID"])
with
        df = df.sort_values([ "zHD", "CID"])  
and note that future unbinned HDs are z-sorted.
CID duplicates are expected ?

comments.body:
This abort is due to a very old default in which EFF(spec) = 1.0 if the user does not specify a spec-Eff map file. Since you did not specify EFF(spec) map, the 100% spec-confirmed sample means that there are no zPHOT events, and thus APPLY_SEARCHEFF_MASK=5 is not possible. The simple fix is to add this into your sim-input file or command line arguments:
   SEARCHEFF_SPEC_FILE:   ZERO 

By explicitly setting EFf(spec) = 0, the zPHOT sample is well defined.

body:
Hi Rick, 
To inform spectroscopic follow-up, we're looking to connect simulated objects with their spectral templates. 
- i.e. for every object simulated, we'd like to know the corresponding .SED file used.  

This fairly straight-forward for the non-Ia population. For each sub-class, we can map the `NON1A_INDEX` column (output by the simulation to a DUMP file) to the corresponding `SED.INFO` file. However, this approach fails for the SNIa-91bg sub-class. These all have `NON1A_INDEX==-9`. 

**For each simulated 91bg, do you know how we can retrieve the SED file used to simulate it?** 

An example output can be found on Perlmutter in `$SCRATCH_SIMDIR/MSTEST_LSSTDDFv34T_SNIa-91bg/`. Looking at the DUMP file, the SED library is `/pscratch/sd/d/desctd/cfs_mirror/SNANA/SURVEYS/LSST/ROOT/PLASTICC/model_libs_updates/SIMSED.SNIa-91bg`, but all of the NON1A_INDEX's are -9. For a CART sample (`$SCRATCH_SIMDIR/MSTEST_LSSTDDFv34T_CART/`) this column is filled. 

Comparing the two, there's no SNIa-91bg_INDEX column in the 91bg SED.INFO file. Could this be the problem? If so, is there a way for me to retrieve the input variables (stretch,color) or filename? I tried adding them to the DUMP file, but they are not available.

Many thanks 

Mat 

p.s. The launch file is `/global/cfs/cdirs/lsst/groups/TD/SN/SNANA/SURVEYS/LSST/USERS/smithmat/tides_sims/inputs/REFAC_SIMGEN_MASTER_LSST_DDF_v34_TEST.INPUT` if required

comments.body:

This is a rather subtle feature that can be avoided. When using submit_batch_jobs.py, the default behavior is to suppress model-specific parameters. The reason is to avoid confusion in the analysis when reading data files in which model parameters suddenly change because GENMODEL changes. under the GENOPT_GLOBAL block as illustrated in

body:
for photo-z light curve fitting with snlc_fit.exe, the intended &FITINP logic is as follows:

OPT_PHOTOZ = 6      !  2=zSpec or 4=quantiles(Cubic interp)
OPT_PHOTOZ = 10.    ! 2=zSpec or 8=quantiles(STEFFEN intern)

However, these "combine" options simply uses zSpec or zPHOT point estimate and ignore the quantiles. OPT_PHOTOZ=4 (or 8) works correctly using only quantiles, and ignoring zSpec. The problem is thus switching from quantiles to zSpec when zSpec is available.

Note that for zPHOT point estimates (ignoring quantiles), OPT_PHOTOZ=2 picks zSpec or zPHOT correctly because REDSHIFT_FINAL is the best redshift among zPHOT and zSPEC. However, selecting among zSpec and quantiles is trickier because they involve different data elements.

comments.body:
The bugs in snlc_fit.car were introduced when MASK_PHOTOZ_SOURCE was introduced a few months ago. This mask is updated each event to determine what redshift source to use, rather than relying on fixed user input OPT_PHOTOZ.

Bug 1:
subroutine FITINI_ZPRIOR was implementing only a single bit of OPT_PHOTOZ; it is now fixed to check quantile bit regardless of whether other bits are set.

Bug 2:
subroutine FITPAR_PREP logic for quantiles was incorrect; see new logic using LPZ_Q

Bug 3:
subroutine FITINI_PHOTOZ was using OPT_PHOTOZ instead of MASK_PHOTOZ_SOURCE.

In addition to these bug fixes, we also updated init_zPDF_spline to return an error_flag for invalid quantiles, rather than abort. This allows snlc_fit to reject such events (ERRFLAG_FIT=4 in SNANA table) and move on. Function dump_zPDF() is called when error_flag is set to enable visual examination of invalid quantiles.

Create_covariance.py already computes COVTOT_INV to check for invertibility, but it was not written out; therefore cosmology fitting programs were needlessly repeating this matrix-inversion computation. As samples (LSST,ROMAN) become larger, this matrix inversion time will take longer, and become particularly annoying when debugging cosmology fitting codes, or running many cosmology fits with different fit option. In addition to writing COVTOT_INV output, also need to
1. add -mucovtot_inv_file argument to wfit.c to read COVTOT_INV and skip matrix inversion
2. add similar option for COSMOISIS
3. update submit_batch_jobs.sh to pass new argument to wfit/Firecrown.

--write_mask_cov 1  # write only covsys
--write_mask_cov 2 # write only covtot_inv


wfit.c has new command line argument 
   "-mucovtot_inv_file" 
and "-mucovsys_file" should replace "-mucov_file" for clarity, although the latter is still accepted for back-compatibility. To read appropriate cov file; see wfit help with wfit.exe | grep mucov

comments.body:
Before investigating abort, need to figure out why submit_batch jobs continued forever. By default, a failure does not trigger "kill_jobs" unless user explicitly specifies the           --kill_on_fail option. The above jobs uses the event-sync option (opt_sncid_list) that requires FITOPT000.FITRES to exist before processing FITOPT001, etc ... So when the first (FITOPT000) fit job fails, the CPU*.CMD script hangs on infinite wait. 

The fix is to internally set args.kill_on_fail = True when event-sync is selected, and to also add a supplement kill_on_fail check in the submit_batch code, in addition to the check in the CPU*.CMD scripts.
The abort seems to be due to a mix-up in defining filters for LOWZ vs. FOUNDATION.

BBC always rejects a small fraction of events due to insufficient sim stats in regions of large stretch and/or color. A larger fraction of events that are kept have biasCor errors that are difficult to quantify. To better sample sparsely populated x1,c regions, biasCor sim should generated using
   PROB(population) -> PROB^ PROB_EXPON_REWGT
where PROB_EXPON_REWGT is a user-input.

body:
While chasing a very subtle bias in the analyzed average of 50 simulated LSST samples, I noticed duplicates in the biasCor sample. The SNIDs are all unique, but SIM_[z,c,x1,a,b] all matched exactly for several events. To diagnose this further, I added this feature to BBC:
   SALT2mu.exe <inputFile>  check_duplicates_biascor=1
which exits after running the check. This check-option works only on command line (interactively) to avoid consuming extra memory in slurm. 

While the data-duplicate check is based on SNID, the biasCor check is based on redshift, color, stretch. For the biasCor sample of 2.8 million events, only 478,000 were unique. The number of duplicates ranges from a few up to 20. In short, the effective size of the biasCor sample here is only about 1/6 of what we wanted.

comments.body:
The underlying problem is rather subtle and seems to be a bit of bad luck picking numbers. First recall how unique SNIDs are chosen among independent sim-jobs running on separate cores. Each sim task has its own JOBID that it uses to re-generate all of the previous random SNIDs (for lower numbered JOBIDs), store them on a list, and then pick new SNIDs that don't overlap the list. The number of randoms stored per event is 3000 (3 lists, 1000 per list), and thus if the number of pre-computed randoms is a multiple of 3000, there will be exact random-sequence overlap between two sim tasks.

The bad luck part was selecting NGENTOT_LC that is a multiple of 1000, and submit_batch adds 1000 to number of generated randoms (NRANGEN) as a safety margin. These multiples of 1000 lead to many sim-tasks pre-computing NRANGEN randoms that is a multiple of 3000.

If we had used NGEN_UNIT, which multiplies a physical rate, the number of events would likely not be a multiple of 1000, thus avoiding the problem.

To greatly reduce such bad-luck numbers, two fixes have been made:
1) MXSTORE_RAN in sim is changed from 1000 to 1001,
2) submit_batch NRANGEN safety margin -> 1013 (instead of 1000)

This seemingly small change breaks the random sequence from previous code versions, and thus about half of the regression tests fail. Some of the SIMFIT fail due to SNID no longer existing in the sim-output. With this change, a new tag must be created ASAP along with a new reference for regression testing.

in function interp_flux_SEDMODEL() (genmag_SEDtools.c), the flux vs. logz was interpolated using a quadratic function. At very late times and high-z, the rest-frame far-UV can vary wildly vs. wavelength, and flux(logz) values such as 
   logz = 0.234700, 0.254719, 0.274738 
   flux = 2.5e+06, 1.7e+05, 1.71e+00
can result in a quadratic fit with negative undershoot that results in negative flux. To avoid negative fluxes for data challenges and image-sim overlays, the fix to avoid is simply to replace quadratic fit with linear fit.

    tmp1 = np.eye(n)

Hi Rick, 

As discussed, we need to change to sigma_tot^2 = sigma_syst^2 + sigma_stat^2, since we are doing sigma_tot = sigma_syst + sigma_stat at the moment. 

```
    for (SNR=10.0; SNR <= 100.0; SNR+= 30.0 ) {
      double PSF_FWHM = 1.0 ; // arcsec
      double x = PSF_FWHM/SNR;
      ANGRES = eval_GENPOLY(x, RESPOLY, fnam);
      printf("\t ANGRES = %7.4f arcsec for SNR = %4.0f (PSF_FWHM=%.1f asec)\n", 
	     ANGRES, SNR, PSF_FWHM); fflush(stdout);

```

This is from line 158 of sntools_sim_atmosphere.c - a simple fix would be to split the eval_GENPOLY output into the constant term (which would be sigma_syst) and the degree >= 1 terms (which would be sigma_stat) => then you could write ANGRES = sqrt(sigma_stat**2 + sigma_syst**2)
But this does assume that the sigma_syst is always a constant term, while sigma_stat has no offset but only the degree >= 1 terms. 

If we want to accept other forms of sigma_syst and sigma_stat, then I think they have to be taken as separate inputs. 

Best, 
Jason

body: Using UVLAM_EXTRAP feature, the original quick-and-dirty safety margin for central wavelength in rest-frame was UVLAM + 700. However, the 700 A safety margin is too large, resulting in unnecessary u-band dropouts at high-z.

comments.body:
A more refined calculation is
   RESTLAMMIN_FILTERCEN =  <LAMOBS_CEN> / ( 1 + zmax)
where zmax = LAMOBS_MIN / UVLAM_EXTRAP - 1

Example with u-band
LAMOBS_CEN = 3700 A (mean of band)
LAMOBS_MIN = 3200 A (blue edge of band)
UVLAM_EXTRAP = 500 A (optional blue-extrapolation)
->
zmax = 5.4
RESTLAMMIN_FILTERCEN = 3700/6.4 = 578 A

This calculated 578 A value is well below the previous ad-hoc 500 + 700 = 1200 A,
and it recovers u-band dropouts.

This revised computation is implemented in genmag_SEDtools.c[h]; see function UVLAM_EXTRAP_RESTLAMMIN_FILTERCEN() for SALT2/SALT3 model. 

NON1ASED models have min filter lam set to 100 A, so was not impacted.

Input files, searcheff, simlib are all on perlmutter at $SNANA_LSST_USERS/gnarayan/YSE/REFAC_SIMGEN_YSE_ZTF_NOBATCH.INPUT

We compiled a version of snlc_sim.exe with a few extra print statements, and then CUTWIN check failed.
We commented out all the CUTWIN cuts in the input file and then uncommented one by one to determine that REDSHIFT cut is the issue. 
We found that output light curves have -9 for the redshift but the SIMLIB has reasonable redshifts - can verify with:
grep REDSHIFT yselc_grizXY_dr1.simlib

So unclear why snlc_sim.exe is ignoring the redshift.

comments.body:
The problem is in the sim-input file and is rather subtle. Start with this grep,

grep SEARCHEFF_ REFAC_SIMGEN_YSE_ZTF_NOBATCH.INPUT 
APPLY_SEARCHEFF_OPT:  1
SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_EFF_FILE: $SNANA_LSST_USERS/gnarayan/YSE/SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_YSE_DR1_SNR4_grizXY.DAT
SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_LOGIC_FILE: $SNANA_LSST_USERS/gnarayan/YSE/SEARCHEFF_PIPELINE_LOGIC_ZTF.DAT
SEARCHEFF_SPEC_FILE:  ZERO
SEARCHEFF_zHOST_FILE:  ZERO

The last two lines state that Eff(spec-confirmation) = 0 and that Eff(zHOST) = 0;  thus there is no source of measuring a redshift, resulting in redshift = -9. The easy fix is to remove the SEARCHEFF_SPEC_FILE line, or override the ZERO argument with
   snlc_sim.exe  REFAC_SIMGEN_YSE_ZTF_NOBATCH.INPUT \
          SEARCHEFF_SPEC_FILE  NONE

If there is no SEARCHEFF_SPEC_FILE key in sim-input, the default EFF(spec-confirmation) = 1.0 and all events will have accurate zSpec.

comments.body:
the sim has no protection against blue-shifts (which are rare, but possible) and it is up to the user to set parameters to avoid this. A simulated blue shift can happen from helio->CMB transformation or from Vpec. In LC fit stage, have you tried
   CUTWIN_REDSHIFT = 0.005, 2.0
I do have CUTWIN_REDSHIFT  =  0.05, 1.2 in the LC fit nml. This is also with data, and I am using header override files for the host galaxy photo-z (which is not zero)

This event has z_spec = 0.9 so it passes CUTWIN_REDHIFT. The issue is that the photo-z estimate is very far off resulting in crazy fitted zphot. Will need to investigate this fit more carefully and hopefully find a robust way to reject it.

FITPROB = 1.335460e-22 for this event, so just change
FITWIN_PROB = 0.0,  1.01
  to
FITWIN_PROB = 0.01,  1.01
SN 1308074 in FITOPTs 2,4,5 also has fitted redshift of 0 with FITPROB 7.82426e-02 so a FITPROB cut is not sufficient

There are two problems with the LC-fit inputs. First, the header override file defined
    HOSTGAL_ZPHOT   HOSTGAL_ZPHOTERR
instead of
   HOSTGAL_PHOTOZ  HOSTGAL_PHOTOZ_ERR
Unfortunately the SNANA codes use a mix of ZPHOT and PHOTOZ conventions, so I added a "mistaken varname" code trap for the override file that will abort and indicate the correct varname to use. 

For FITOPT002 with OPT_PHOTOZ=1, the 2nd problem is that PRIOR_ZERRSCALE was not specified and thus the default value of 1000 essentially made the host photo-z prior a flat prior. Setting PRIOR_ZERRSCALE=1 results in reasonable output for SNID= 1308074

PRIOR_ZERRSCALE likely does not impact quantiles, but it does impact using photo-z mean and STD as prior.

for SNID= 1304045, the real zSpec = 0.8, so with photo-z ~ 0 the fitted stretch x1=4.6 is way outside the nominal bound of |x1| < 3
How is it possible that the best fit photo-z is 0 though? The host priors are ~0.3, 0.15 for DNF, BPZ respectively, so it's unclear how the chi2 would be favored at z=0

the host photo-z ~ .2 is very far away from the true zSpec ~ 0.8, so it's not clear how the photo-z fit behaves in such a pathological situation. The real stretch is multiplied by 1+z = 1.8 for the observer frame, and with photo-z ~ 0 the fitted stretch absorbs 1+zSpec and is thus unphysical.
Okay, any recommendation for how to cut these kinds of pathological fits? Just raising the minimum FITPROB?

A combination of cuts on FITPROB, color, stretch will hopefully remove pathological fits. Rather than identifying one event at a time, can you analyze a large sample and try to find ~dozen(s) of them?

body: For COVADD option (BBC method using SALT2mu.exe code), the bias-correction was applied before sigInt map was made and thus 1/MUERR^2 weight was incorrect. This is essentially a chicken and egg problem; computing COVADD term needs b iasCor, but biasCor needs COVADD for 1/MUERR^2 weight. The COVSCALE method doesn't have this problem because SIGINT is computed from SNRMAX>60 events and does not need biasCor map.

comments.body:
Resolution is to use the original COVSCALE method to get initial 1/MUERR^2 weight. Use this approx weight to compute biasCor for creating COVADD map and then zero out SIGINT used for scale.  Restore bug with 
   restore_bug2_mucovadd=1

This is an order of operation bug.
In slide 5/6/7 of these [GOODLE SLIDES](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1ynHsMg0oFswleKMQPQUvmW772ZPc-nxsi9HOGa8f4nE/edit?usp=sharing) we talk about why things were different and how we fixed the problem

This fix was tricky because data files don't contain quantiles and thus the default override procedure doesn't even check the quantiles. Even if the data includes quantiles, the number of override quantiles could be different than the original. I therefore added a new rd_override_zphot_q() function (in sntools_data.c) that always forces an override regardless of whether quantiles exist or not.

To select events on the override list,
&SNLCINP
HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE =        '$DES_USERS/rebeccachen/PZQ/hostlibs/data_sompz_override.HOSTLIB'
SNCID_LIST_FILE   = 
   '$DES_USERS/rebeccachen/PZQ/hostlibs/data_sompz_override.HOSTLIB'

where the argument is the same for HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE and SNCID_LIST_FILE. There is no need to construct a separate CID list file. To more robustly select events from an override file, I added this new feature,
      SNCID_LIST_FILE  = 'HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE'
will internally replaces HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE with its argument. Thus the HEADER_OVERRIDE_FILE argument can be altered and the SNCID_LIST_FILE is automatically synced.

Hi,
I think it's not exactly DL = (1+zHEL) * rz with zHEL including vpec, because relativistic beaming add a (1 + v/c)^2 to DL (eq 18 https://arxiv.org/pdf/1012.2912.pdf). Hence if zHEL already contains the peculiar velocity DL = (1 + zHEL) * (1 + v/c) rz = (1 + zCMB) * (1+ zOURPV)  * (1 + zPV) ^2 * rz where zOURPV is our velocity from CMB dipole.
Hi, any update on this issue?

comments.body: please clarify "result in conflicting best fits for alpha & beta". What is the probem?

Yeah no worries, so for the example linked above, when I use 
```
p1 = 0.155
p2 = 2.87
```
in my BBC input file, the best fit alpha and beta are:
```
alpha0:	  0.15691  0.00319
beta0:    2.94093  0.03226
```
However, when I use 
```
p1 = 0.140
p2 = 3.10
```
in the same BBC input file, only changing p1 & p2, the best fit alpha and beta are:
```
alpha0:       0.14299  0.00318 
beta0:        3.17986  0.03158 
```
The initial values of p1 & p2 seem to significantly impact the results.

I think the problem is that for BS21 model, BBC's p2 input is not just the initial beta value, but there is an old BBC hack using p2 as the true fitted sim-beta for the biasCor sample ... because we don't know how to compute a true fitted-beta for BS21 model. Thus changing p2 (initial beta value) can change the BBC-fitted results.

comments.body:
Recently, the gzipping of INPUT_FITOPT*.FITRES files was modified to gzip more quickly by doing parallel gzip with groups of 10 files. The problem above is that the number of files per group is 10 10 10 10 4 ... and the only the last gzip command did NOT have ampersand to force waiting before returning control to submit_batch. Gzipping 4 files is quicker than gzipping 10 files, and thus submit_batch moved on before all files were gzipped.

Two fixes were made. First, the gzip file groups are submitted in reverse order so that the group with missing ampersand (wait for gzip to finish) always has 10 files. Second, after control is returned to submit_batch, it counts the number of existing .gz files and doesn't return until the expected number of .gz files exists.

in $DES_ROOT/simlibs/FLUXERRMODEL_maps/FLUXERRMODEL_SIM.DAT
everything works... so it's a problem with REDCOV

The underlying bug is that the sim was writing the cumulative field list for each epoch, instead of the field for each epoch. For for field overlaps, when field list becomes e.g.,  C2+C3, this C2+C3 string was written as the field epoch instead of C3. The C2+C3 field was not recognized in any REDCOV map and thus returned an error scale of 1, which resulted in COV matrix elements of zero ... which is not pos definite. 

Anticipating a related bug in the future, if the FLUXERRMODEL_FILE includes error scales that are exactly 1.000, the sim code replaces 1.00 with 1.01 to avoid GSL error "matrix not pos definite".

body: Running LCFIT on 50 sim-data samples with dozens of systematics results in few E5 files piling up in /SPLIT_JOBS, which can slow the merge process with file-system access issues. Another problem is that the slowest core always does the merge and thus falls further behind.

comments.body:
For all classes, no more than 10 merge tasks will run before exiting, thus allowing other cores to better share the CPU burden. The last core must finish everything and thus has no merge task limit.

To reduce file-count in SPLIT_JOBS (LCFIT class), each set of  SPLIT files is tarred and deleted during merge process. With 25 split jobs, the number of LOG/YAML/DONE/TEXT files is reduced by almost a factor of 25.

Added another trick when scanning MERGE.LOG and checking for LCFIT-DONE files: if FITOPTnnn is not completed, then the remaining FITOPTs are not searched and the merge process skips to next version. This algorithm avoids needlessly scanning DONE files for FITOPTs that are not finished.

OUTPUT_BBCFIT-0027/FITOPT009_MUOPT000.FITRES.gz:# WARNING(MINOR): 16 fit M0ERR had crazy values --> fit repeated.
OUTPUT_BBCFIT-0046/FITOPT000_MUOPT000.FITRES.gz:# WARNING(MINOR): 20 fit M0ERR had crazy values --> fit repeated.
OUTPUT_BBCFIT-0046/FITOPT007_MUOPT000.FITRES.gz:# WARNING(MINOR): 20 fit M0ERR had crazy values --> fit repeated.

The repeated fit values look sensible by eye … and clearly way more sensible than the crazy errors from the first fit attempt that resulted in w=-1.5 for sample 0046. These warnings are flagged as MINOR. If crazy small errors persist after 2nd fit attempt, the warning message is SEVERE and non-zero NWARN_CRAZYERR is written to YAML output.

My hunch is that this crazy-error feature has been unknowingly causing problems in previous many-sample tests since there was no clear way to flag it other than MUERR_RENORM/MUERR << 1 (opposite of too-big MUERR_RENORM issue posted yesterday on git issue)

When working with large bias sims, you will sometimes produces supernovae with large `muErrsq` values, especially when working with the C11 intrinsic scatter model.

This will then produce an error in the BIASCOR stage in `output_ITER1/FAIL_SUMMARY.LOG` similar to the following:
```
FAILURE-0001:
  JOB_LOG_FILE:       OUTPUT_BBCFIT_FITOPT000_MUOPT001.LOG
  FAIL_REPEAT_SCRIPT: FAIL_REPEAT_OUTPUT_BBCFIT_FITOPT000_MUOPT001.CMD
  FAIL_MODE:          ABORT
  ABORT_MESSAGES:
  - FATAL ERROR ABORT called by makeMap_sigmu_biasCor
  - Invalid muErrsq=106.055891 for ievt=617323 (SNID=8257957)
  - Something is messed up.
```
This in turn produces an error in `output/FAIL_SUMMARY.LOG` similar to:
```
FAILURE-0001:
  JOB_LOG_FILE:       OUTPUT_BBCFIT_FITOPT000_MUOPT002.LOG
  FAIL_REPEAT_SCRIPT: FAIL_REPEAT_OUTPUT_BBCFIT_FITOPT000_MUOPT002.CMD
  FAIL_MODE:          ABORT
  ABORT_MESSAGES:
  - FATAL ERROR ABORT called by match_cidlist_init
  - CID TABLE DOES NOT EXIST
  - Check file /scratch/midway2/rkessler/PIPPIN_OUTPUT/PA_D5YR_SIM/6_BIASCOR/P21NOM_SIGINT_COLOR/output_ITER1/OUTPUT_BBCFIT/BBC_ACCEPT_SUMMARY.LIST
```

The solution at the moment is to go to the `MERGE` output, find the `FITOPT*.gz` file containing the offending `SNID`, delete that line, and run BBC again. This process will sometimes need to be repeated twice or thrice, taking up a lot of time.

I propose that if a supernova is found with an Invalid muErrsq, it is simply ignored and added to a list of invalid supernovae. This list can then be reported as a warning for further investigation. If this list becomes very large (say, 1% of the total number of supernovae) then it would be reasonable to crash, but at that point you'd know every supernovae with an invalid muErrsq, not just one.

Currently we can specify if we'd like to use the 2d Milky Way extinction map for a model and the E(B-V) value used to correct photometry for extinction is dumped to an output file as MWEBV. This means that if a model config specifies to not use Milky Way extinction, then zero MWEBV value will be written. It affects Elasticc models (d-sct, Cepheid, M-dwarf flare, dwarf novae) which turn off SNANA extinction correction and provides light curves corrected by extinction using 3-d dust maps.

I propose to always output 2-d MWEBV values and explicitly say in the documentation that it is just a function of the spherical coordinates.

comments.body: Can you provide MWEBV in the library parameter list so that the simulation can automatically know to write nominal MWEBV without actually applying it. The sim is often used to explicitly turn off MWEBV, so the sim needs a clear flag to implement this new feature.
What do you mean by MWEBV here? The actual value used or SFD value? The first case doesn't solve Elasticc challenge problem: this value (as well as e.g. true redshift) is not known for real objects.

In the LCLIB file, please add actual MWEBV used. It serves two purposes: 1) provides true MWEBV for later analysis, and 2) it's a flag for simulation to write SFD98 MWEBV into header but NOT apply it.
We will do it. Maybe it should be some other name, for example EBV or extinction? I think users can be confused by the fact that LCLIB specifies one MWEBV, while output contains another one
and note that MWEBV from LCLIB is automatically renamed to avoid confusion.
This is a very good documentation change, thank you

body:
SED Python module implementation uses lists to pass numerical data from Python to C, but it looks like the actual python models use numpy internally, so back-and-force transformation `numpy array -> python list -> double *` happens. It is not a fast thing to do: 1) we create a lot of Python float objects at the first step 2) we slowly access list elements on the second step. For example for 10000 (`MXLAM_PySEDMODEL` value) element array it takes ~0.4ms, so for simulating a light curve with Nobs=1000 it would spend ~0.4s  just doing these transformations:
```python
In [1]: x = np.arange(10000)
In [2]: %timeit np.array(list(x))
390 µs ± 2.85 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000 loops each)
```

I suggest to use the buffer protocol instead and return numpy arrays from Python methods (or any other objects supporting the protocol)
https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/buffer.html

comments.body: Please provide a working example with the AGN model code. The conversion to python list is not ideal, but was reliable and worked with the SNANA C code.

title: Use buffer protocol to pass data from Python SED modules

body: for BBC event syncing among systematics, FITOPT000 must complete before any of the FITOPT[nnn] run with nnn>0. This feature is implemented with explicit file-wait command in the CPU*.CMD files. For jobs that have many data versions and systematics, there is recent evidence of a rare case in which the wait time is infinite because the merge process didn't run to create the OUTPUT-FITRES file that is required to continue. I think this is an artifact of multiple BUSY files that prevent the required merge-task.

comments.body: A hopeful fix was added in which a "--merge_force" command is given to the BBC merge task (FITOPT000) that produces an output FITRES file required to continue. The merge_force causes the merge process to wait for BUSY files to clear, which should guarantee that a merge process produces the required output FITRES file. Note that the nominal --merge command exits immediately if there is another merge task running (i.e., a BUSY file already exists).
